BOGOTA, Colombia (CNN) -- A former Colombian congressman who was held hostage in the jungle for more than eight years has escaped -- with the help of a former captor. Oscar Tulio Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. Oscar Tulio Lizcano, his hair disheveled, appeared too weak to stand for long when he met the news media Sunday, hours after stumbling onto a military patrol -- and freedom. Lizcano suffered from hunger and disease in captivity and endured isolation in the company of leftist rebels who often would not let him talk, he and Colombian authorities said. "Maybe my incoherence is for a lack of speaking," Lizcano told reporters. "I was unable to talk with the guerillas who guarded me." Lizcano said he had little to read in the jungle except "The Odyssey" by Homer. He suffered from malaria and other illnesses and once ate nothing but hearts of palm for six or seven days, said Juan Manuel Santos, the Colombian defense minister. "This is big news for the whole family," said Lizcano's sister, Amparo Lizcano. "We were waiting for the guerrillas to give our brother back alive before he died." The former congressman fled about three days ago with the assistance of one of his captors, a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, a leftist rebel force that has been fighting the government for more than 40 years in a war that also has involved right-wing paramilitaries and drug traffickers.  Watch release of FARC hostage » . President Alvaro Uribe appeared on television Sunday with the ex-FARC rebel -- known by the alias "Isaza" -- and said the man will receive compensation and permission to resettle in France with his family. He said that's in keeping with a Colombian government policy that rewards rebels who desert and help hostages gain their freedom. Police officers and soldiers pinpointed the location of the FARC unit holding Lizcano several months ago, Santos said. They monitored the location for about five months and took steps to seal off possible escape routes, he said, as they planned a rescue operation using information gleaned help from a rebel who deserted October 2. Troops started that rescue operation Saturday -- only to discover that "Isaza" and Lizcano had decided on their own to escape. The two men wandered through the jungle for three days and nights before encountering a Colombian army patrol Sunday, said Santos, the defense minister. Lizcano was kidnapped on August 4, 2000 near the Colombian town of Riosucio. He and his former captor stumbled Sunday onto a patrol near the border of the states of Risaralda and Choco, in central Colombia, authorities said. The FARC holds an estimated 750 hostages in Colombia. Its members have justified hostage taking as a legitimate military tactic. The rebels have been battered this year by government raids that killed several top commanders, the death by apparent heart attack of their founder and a wave of desertions. Government commandoes tricked the FARC in July and freed their most prized hostage, the former presidential candidate Ingrid Betancourt, in an elaborate ruse that also liberated three U.S. defense contractors and 11 other hostages. On Sunday, Lizcano offered words of encouragement to those hundreds who remain trapped in the jungle, captives of the FARC. "Hold on. Hold on," he said. "One day you will enjoy your freedom, too." -- CNN's Karl Penhaul contributed to this report .

The ex-lawmaker made his escape approximately three days earlier, helped by one of his guards—a member of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, known as FARC. On Sunday, President Alvaro Uribe made a televised appearance alongside the former FARC guerrilla, who goes by the codename "Isaza." The pair spent three days and three nights making their way through the jungle before coming across a Colombian army patrol on Sunday, the defense minister said. Officials reported that Lizcano, seized on August 4, 2000, near Riosucio, and his former guard encountered the patrol close to the boundary between the states of Risaralda and Choco in central Colombia.

# Hostages Flee FARC Captivity in Colombian Jungle; Rescue Revives Memory of Betancourt Case

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — Several hostages held by leftist rebels escaped from a jungle camp in southern Colombia this week, slipping away from their captors during a chaotic firefight with government troops, military officials said Thursday.

The escape, which unfolded over several days in the dense forests of Caquetá department, marked the latest chapter in Colombia's long struggle with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, the guerrilla group that for decades made kidnapping a central tactic of its insurgency.

## A Desperate Flight Through the Jungle

According to accounts provided by military officials, the captives fled during a moment of confusion as security forces closed in on the rebel encampment. The hostages, some of whom had reportedly been held for years, traversed difficult terrain before making contact with an army patrol.

"They walked for hours, exhausted and malnourished, but determined to reach freedom," a regional military commander said, speaking on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to discuss operational details. The former captives were receiving medical attention and had been reunited with relatives, officials added.

The identities of those who escaped were not immediately released, pending notification of families and security assessments.

## Decades of Kidnapping

The FARC, founded in 1964 as a Marxist peasant movement, financed its insurgency through kidnapping, extortion and the drug trade during a conflict that has killed more than 220,000 people and displaced millions.

At the height of its power in the late 1990s and early 2000s, the group held hundreds of hostages, including politicians, soldiers, police officers and foreign nationals. Many were kept in makeshift jungle camps for years, chained at night and moved constantly to evade rescue operations.

## The Betancourt Precedent

The most famous rescue came in July 2008, when Colombian military intelligence orchestrated Operation Jaque — a bloodless ruse in which agents posing as aid workers persuaded rebels to hand over 15 hostages for a supposed transfer.

Among those freed was Ingrid Betancourt, a French-Colombian politician who had been kidnapped in 2002 while campaigning for the presidency. Her more than six years in captivity, and the international campaign for her release, made her the world's best-known symbol of Colombia's hostage crisis.

Also freed in that operation were three American defense contractors held since 2003 and 11 members of the Colombian security forces.

The Betancourt rescue was widely seen as a turning point that weakened the FARC's leverage and momentum, contributing to a series of military setbacks for the rebels.

## Toward Peace, and Its Limits

The Colombian government signed a landmark peace accord with the FARC in 2016, leading most of the group's fighters to demobilize and form a political party. The agreement was hailed internationally and earned then-President Juan Manuel Santos the Nobel Peace Prize.

But dissident factions rejected the deal and continue to operate in remote regions, financing themselves through drug trafficking, illegal mining and, in some cases, a return to kidnapping. Other armed groups, including the National Liberation Army, or ELN, remain active as well.

Human rights organizations say kidnappings, while sharply reduced from their peak, have persisted and even ticked upward in some areas, underscoring the fragile nature of Colombia's peace.

## An Uncertain Peace

For the families of those who escaped this week, the ordeal offered a reminder that, more than a half-century after the conflict began, the shadow of Colombia's armed groups has not fully lifted.

Government officials pledged to continue military operations against holdout factions while pursuing negotiations with armed groups still willing to talk.

"Every hostage who returns home is a victory," the regional commander said. "But our work is not finished until no family in Colombia has to wonder whether a loved one will come back from the jungle."

---

# Colombian Politician Escapes After More Than Eight Years in Rebel Captivity

**BOGOTÁ, Colombia** — A Colombian politician who spent more than eight years as a hostage in the country's dense jungle has escaped his captors, emerging gaunt but alive in what officials are calling a remarkable act of survival and courage.

Authorities confirmed that the former regional councilman, whose kidnapping had faded from headlines over the years, walked to freedom early yesterday after fleeing during a rebel unit's overnight movement through rugged terrain in the country's southeastern jungle region.

## A Long Ordeal Ends

The politician, held since his abduction more than eight years ago, was located by a military patrol after wandering for several days. Medical personnel described his condition as fragile but stable.

"He is severely malnourished and suffering from multiple untreated tropical infections, but he is alive, and he is going to recover," said a physician who examined him upon his arrival at a regional hospital. "The human will to survive is extraordinary. This man should not be standing, and yet here he is."

Photographs released by authorities showed a thin, bearded man with sunken eyes, wrapped in a blanket, being helped from a military helicopter.

## "I Never Stopped Believing"

Speaking briefly to reporters from his hospital bed, his voice weak but steady, the freed hostage described years of chains, forced marches, and isolation.

"There were nights I did not think I would see morning," he said. "But I never stopped believing that one day I would walk out of that jungle and hold my family again. Today that day has come."

He paused, visibly emotional. "To those still held out there — do not lose hope. Do not let them take your spirit, even when they take everything else."

## The Rebel Who Helped

In an unexpected turn, officials revealed that a young guerrilla fighter — disillusioned with the armed group and its cause — aided in the escape and surrendered alongside the hostage.

The defector, a low-ranking member described as being in his early twenties, reportedly loosened the politician's restraints and guided him toward a river the two followed until reaching safety.

"I did not join to guard prisoners in the mud until they died," the young man told investigators, according to a military spokesman. "I wanted a different life. Helping him escape was the first free thing I have ever done."

Authorities said the defector will be processed under the country's demobilization program and could receive protection in exchange for his cooperation.

## A Family's Reunion

The politician's family, who had campaigned for years to keep his case alive, rushed to the hospital upon hearing the news.

"We prayed for this every single day," a family member said through tears. "We were told to prepare for the worst so many times. God gave him back to us."

## Ongoing Concerns

Officials say the escape may offer new intelligence about other hostages still believed to be held in remote camps. Human rights organizations renewed calls for the release of all remaining captives.

"Every hostage freed is a victory," said one advocate. "But we cannot rest while others remain chained in the jungle."

The freed politician is expected to remain hospitalized for several weeks as he recovers.
